passage:
Every September, a little before dark, the chimney swifts of Wenbury gather over the old Linden Row School. The sun drops behind Calder Ridge, the bank on Mill Street pulls down its shutters, the church clock strikes seven and the last children leave the schoolyard, and still the birds wheel overhead in a dark, turning cloud. Then the last bus passes the school gates, and the whole cloud pours down into the chimney like smoke running backwards; by the time the streetlights on the hill come on, the sky is clear.

Tomas Reyburn was caretaker at Linden Row for thirty years, and he lit the school's furnace every winter morning until the day the school closed, eleven years ago. Since 1996 he has stood in the schoolyard each September evening with a hand counter, and his notebooks show the roost holding steady at about five thousand birds. Of all his stories, the one he tells most often is about that furnace.

It was the first September after the school closed. Walking home past Linden Row at dusk, Reyburn saw a dark plume over the chimney, ran to the boiler room with a fire bucket, and flung open the furnace door to find the grate cold and swifts pattering down the flue. He tells it laughing, and he always slaps his knee at the part with the bucket. When the storm two winters ago put a crack near the chimney's top, the council voted to mend it and keep it standing, just as Reyburn had said it would, and the masons did the work in lime mortar rather than cheap cement, rough as the old brick.

I laughed out loud the first evening I saw it myself: a chimney that has burned nothing for eleven years, drawing a cloud of smoke down into itself.

In early October the birds will leave for the south, and the chimney will stand cold until they return in May. Until they go, every clear evening the old chimney smokes in reverse over the schoolyard, and I stand at the gate grinning up at it.
